chapter.name: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity

questions.q: Bhavisha stands before a tall iron pillar at Mehrauli in Delhi that has stood in the open for over 1,600 years without rusting. In the reign of which ruler was this pillar erected?
questions.a: Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty
o: Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty
Chandragupta I of the Gupta dynasty
Chandragupta Maurya of the Maurya dynasty

questions.q: Which change in the 3rd century CE set the stage for the Gupta dynasty to rise to power?
questions.a: The Kushana Empire in the north and northwest of the subcontinent began to weaken.
o: The Kushana Empire in the north and northwest of the subcontinent began to weaken.
The Huna tribe from Central Asia began to attack north India.
The Satavahanas moved their capital to the Gangetic plains.
The Pallavas conquered the kingdoms around Pataliputra.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Iron Pillar of Delhi is linked with the god Vishnu.
Reason (R): Chandragupta II, in whose reign the pillar was erected, was a devotee of Vishnu.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the early Gupta rulers.
I. Chandragupta I is remembered for his coins and his strategic alliances.
II. Chandragupta II was a devotee of Shiva, and Shiva's bull Nandi often appears on his inscriptions.
III. On the reverse of a gold coin of Chandragupta I is a seated goddess identified as Lakshmi.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: True or False: 'Chandragupta II of the Gupta dynasty and Chandragupta Maurya are two different rulers.' Give a reason for your answer.
questions.a: True. Chandragupta II, also called Vikramaditya, belonged to the Gupta dynasty, while Chandragupta Maurya belonged to the earlier Maurya dynasty; the chapter warns us not to confuse the two.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: Chandragupta II was a Gupta ruler (Vikramaditya), Chandragupta Maurya was of the Maurya dynasty

questions.q:
(a) By what other name was Chandragupta II known?
(b) Name the mount (vahana) of Vishnu that often appears on Chandragupta II's inscriptions.
questions.a: (a) Vikramaditya. (b) Garuda.
s: (a) Names Vikramaditya
(b) Names Garuda

questions.q: A guidebook says: 'The Iron Pillar has always stood at Mehrauli, where Chandragupta II had it made as a monument for his capital.' Point out three errors in this sentence, using the chapter.
questions.a: Any three distinct errors: (1) It has not always stood at Mehrauli: it was probably first erected in front of the Udayagiri caves (Madhya Pradesh) and brought to Delhi only a few centuries later. (2) It was not made as a monument for a capital: it was dedicated to Vishnu, and its inscriptions celebrate the king's achievements. (3) Delhi was not the Gupta capital; the capital was Pataliputra (present-day Patna).
s: Error on place: probably first stood at Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh), brought to Delhi a few centuries later
Error on purpose: dedicated to Vishnu; inscriptions celebrate the king's achievements
Error on capital: the Gupta capital was Pataliputra (Patna), not Delhi

questions.q:
In 2026 the heritage club of a Delhi school builds a timeline wall. A tour guide at Mehrauli tells them the Iron Pillar is 'over 1,600 years old' and was erected in the reign of Chandragupta II. Their timeline already has two cards: 'Kushana Empire starts to weaken: 3rd century CE' and 'Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya: around 500 CE'.
(a) Taking the guide's figure as true in 2026, before which year CE must the pillar have been erected?
(b) How was Chandragupta II related to Chandragupta I?
(c) Riya wants to put the pillar card before the Kushana card. Explain why the chapter does not allow this.
(d) Raghav says the pillar is older than the Aryabhatiya. Is the data enough to decide? Justify with numbers.
questions.a: (a) 2026 - 1600 = 426, so it was erected before about 426 CE. (b) Chandragupta I was his grandfather (Chandragupta II is his grandson). (c) The Guptas rose only after the Kushana Empire began to weaken by the 3rd century CE, and the pillar belongs to the reign of Chandragupta II, two generations after Chandragupta I laid the foundation; so the pillar card must come after the Kushana card. (d) Yes. The pillar is from before about 426 CE and the Aryabhatiya is from around 500 CE, so the pillar is older by at least about 74 years (500 - 426); Raghav is right.
s: (a) Computes 2026 - 1600 = 426: erected before about 426 CE
(b) Chandragupta I was Chandragupta II's grandfather
(c) Guptas rose after the Kushana decline, and the pillar is from a later Gupta reign, so it comes after the Kushana card
(d) Yes: before about 426 CE versus around 500 CE, at least about 74 years older

questions.q:
Answer these questions about the Iron Pillar of Delhi.
(a) In which part of Delhi does it stand today?
(b) About how much does it weigh?
(c) To which god was it dedicated?
(d) Where was it probably first erected?
(e) A bicycle left in the rain for one year shows rust. Explain in one sentence why the pillar does not rust.
questions.a: (a) Mehrauli. (b) About 6 tonnes. (c) Vishnu. (d) In front of the Udayagiri caves in Madhya Pradesh. (e) Scientists believe a thin layer, formed by the special iron used and oxygen from the air, covers its surface and protects it from corrosion.
s: (a) Mehrauli
(b) About 6 tonnes
(c) Vishnu
(d) In front of the Udayagiri caves, Madhya Pradesh
(e) A thin protective layer formed by the special iron and oxygen from the air

questions.q: Who wrote the Prayaga Prashasti, the pillar inscription at Prayagraj that praises the achievements of Samudragupta?
questions.a: Harisena, the court poet
o: Kalidasa, the poet of the Meghadutam

questions.q: In a classroom role-play, King X fights Samudragupta, loses, and gets his throne back by paying tribute. King Y, fearing Samudragupta's might, submits without a fight. Going by the Prayaga Prashasti, which statement fits BOTH kings?
questions.a: Both ended up accepting Samudragupta as their overlord.
o: Both ended up accepting Samudragupta as their overlord.
Both had their kingdoms taken over and added to the Gupta Empire.
Neither had to accept Samudragupta's supremacy.
Both were Pallava rulers from the south.

questions.q:
Match each source in Column A with what it tells us in Column B.
Column A: 1. Prayaga Prashasti  2. A coin of Samudragupta seated with a veena  3. A coin showing a sacrificial horse  4. Vishnu Purana
Column B: A. An ashvamedha yajna was commemorated  B. The king's wars and his ambition to unify the Earth  C. The key regions the Gupta dynasty would rule  D. The king as a player of music

(a) What does the phrase 'dharani-bandha' mean?
(b) According to the Prayaga Prashasti, whose ambition was it?
questions.a: (a) To unify the Earth. (b) Samudragupta's.
s: (a) To unify the Earth
(b) Samudragupta

questions.q: Apart from his wars, Harisena praises Samudragupta for supporting certain fields. Name any two of them and state what this support did for his kingdom.
questions.a: Any two of art, learning and trade; this support made his kingdom rich and successful.
s: Names any two of art, learning and trade
States that it made his kingdom rich and successful

questions.q:
(a) Where is the Prayaga Prashasti found?
(b) Samudragupta was the father of which famous Gupta ruler?
(c) One of his coins shows him playing the veena. What does this suggest about him besides being a warrior?
questions.a: (a) On a pillar in Prayagraj. (b) Chandragupta II. (c) That he loved or valued music and the arts; Harisena also says he supported art and learning.
s: (a) On a pillar at Prayagraj
(b) Chandragupta II
(c) He valued music and the arts, not only war

questions.q: Samudragupta did not take over every kingdom he defeated; many defeated kings were reinstated and paid him tribute. Using the chapter, explain (a) one gain for Samudragupta from tribute, (b) how tributary kings helped his marching army, (c) where the same policy appears again in the south or the northeast, and (d) one possible risk the policy could carry for the empire later (a reasoned guess).
questions.a: (a) Tribute brought him wealth without the cost of governing every kingdom directly. (b) The chapter reasons that tributary kings must have been asked to provide for his huge army of soldiers, elephants, horses, cooks and support staff and the supplies to feed them. (c) He defeated a Pallava ruler and the ruler of Kamarupa but let them keep their thrones as long as they accepted his rule and paid tribute. (d) Reasoned inference (the chapter does not make this link itself): rulers who kept their thrones also kept their own power and could grow strong; the chapter notes that by the 6th century CE the rise of powerful regional rulers led to internal conflicts. Accept any sensible risk.
s: (a) Tribute gave wealth without ruling every kingdom directly
(b) Tributary kings supplied the army (men, animals, food)
(c) Pallava or Kamarupa rulers kept their thrones on accepting his rule and paying tribute
(d) Any sensible risk, e.g. local rulers kept power and could grow strong (reasoned inference)

questions.q:
A Patna school is making a wall map titled 'The Gupta Empire'. Its notes say: the Vishnu Purana lists four regions the Gupta dynasty will rule; the map in the chapter notes that the Vakatakas were allies of the Guptas, and that the Guptas claim to have conquered parts of the east coast down to the Pallavas, whom they may have briefly subdued.
(a) Name the four regions the Vishnu Purana lists.
(b) Why is a map of only these four regions too small for the empire at its peak?
(c) Should the Vakataka kingdom be coloured as Gupta territory? Give a reason.
(d) The team can colour the east coast down to the Pallavas either in full Gupta colour or in a lighter shade with a note. Which is the better choice? Justify using the wording of the notes.
questions.a: (a) Anuganga (the middle-Gangetic basin), Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha. (b) At its peak the empire covered most of present-day north and west India and parts of central and east India, far more than these four regions. (c) No; the Vakatakas were allies of the Guptas, not a conquered part of the empire. (d) The lighter shade with a note, because the source only says the Guptas 'claim' this conquest and 'may have briefly' subdued the Pallavas; full colour would present an uncertain, possibly short-lived claim as firm, lasting rule.
s: (a) Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha
(b) At its peak the empire covered most of north and west India and parts of central and east India
(c) No: the Vakatakas were allies, not conquered land
(d) Lighter shade with a note, because 'claim' and 'may have briefly subdued' show the control was uncertain

questions.q: Samudragupta and his age appear in several sources. For each of the four below, state what it tells us: (a) the Prayaga Prashasti, about Samudragupta, (b) the coin showing him with a veena, about Samudragupta, (c) the ashvamedha coin shown in the chapter, about a king's ambitions, (d) the Vishnu Purana, about the Gupta empire. Then (e) state one reason a historian should be careful about the Prayaga Prashasti.
questions.a: (a) He fought many wars, took over some kingdoms, reinstated defeated kings who paid tribute, wanted to unify the Earth, and supported art, learning and trade. (b) He is shown as a veena player, so he valued music. (c) Such a coin, showing the sacrificial horse, commemorated an ashvamedha yajna, which ambitious kings performed to build mighty empires and leave a legacy, so it tells us the king who minted it had imperial ambitions. (d) It names the key regions of the Gupta empire: Anuganga, Prayaga, Saketa and Magadha. (e) It was written by Harisena, Samudragupta's own court poet, to praise the king, so it shows only the court's side and needs checking against other sources.
s: (a) Prashasti: wars, tribute, ambition to unify the Earth, support for arts and trade
(b) Veena coin: he valued music
(c) Ashvamedha coin: marks a horse sacrifice performed by ambitious kings to build empires
(d) Vishnu Purana: key regions of the empire
(e) Written by his court poet to praise him, so it needs other sources

questions.q: The Chinese traveller Faxian set out on a long pilgrimage to India in the early 5th century CE. Which of these was NOT one of the purposes of his journey?
questions.a: To collect taxes on behalf of the Gupta king
o: To collect taxes on behalf of the Gupta king
To learn from renowned Indian scholars
To collect manuscripts of Buddhist texts to take back to China

questions.q: Faxian's travelogue, translated into English by J. Legge, has survived to this day. What is it called?
questions.a: A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Faxian's travelogue shows that every group in Gupta society was treated well.
Reason (R): Elsewhere in his travelogue, Faxian describes the harsh treatment of the chandalas, who were regarded as outcastes and lived outside the city limits.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
(a) From which country did Faxian come?
(b) Give one reason why his travelogue is useful to us today.
questions.a: (a) China. (b) It has survived to this day and records what he observed of the culture, governance and society of India in the Gupta age.
s: (a) China
(b) It survives and records his observations of Gupta-age society and governance

questions.q:
Faxian writes that 'the king's guards and attendants have salaries'.
(a) What does this tell us about how the Gupta state treated the people who served it?
(b) Name the main source of revenue from which the state could have paid such salaries.
questions.a: (a) The state paid its guards and attendants regular salaries, which points to an organised administration. (b) Land tax, the primary source of Gupta revenue (revenue was used for administration and the army).
s: (a) Staff were paid regular salaries by an organised state
(b) Land tax, the main source of revenue

questions.q: Kavya reads Faxian's line that the people 'have no need to register households or attend to officials'. She then reads that the Guptas recorded their land grants carefully on copper plates to ensure proper tax collection. She says, 'These two sources contradict each other, so one of them must be false.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The two statements are about different things: Faxian speaks of ordinary people not having to register their households, while the copper plates record grants of land to local rulers, priests and chieftains. Also, Faxian's account reflects only his own perspective, at one time, for a limited part of society. Historians do not throw out one source; they compare several sources to build a fuller picture.
s: Verdict: No, they need not contradict
The sources describe different things: households of ordinary people versus land grants to local rulers, priests and chieftains
Faxian's view is partial; historians compare sources rather than discard one

questions.q:
A Class 7 group in Chennai reads this extract from Faxian's record of the Gupta age (early 5th century CE): 'The people are numerous and happy ... Those who farm royal land pay a portion of their grain ... The king's guards and attendants have salaries ... Heads of Vaishya families establish houses for charity and medicines ... the poor, orphans and the sick are cared for.'
(a) According to the extract, who pays a portion of their grain?
(b) Who receives salaries?
(c) Who sets up houses for charity and medicines?
(d) Name the group that Faxian describes elsewhere as harshly treated, and say where they lived.
questions.a: (a) Those who farm royal land. (b) The king's guards and attendants. (c) Heads of Vaishya families, that is, merchants or traders. (d) The chandalas, regarded as outcastes, who lived outside the city limits.
s: (a) Farmers of royal land
(b) The king's guards and attendants
(c) Heads of Vaishya (merchant) families
(d) The chandalas, living outside the city limits

questions.q: A historian has two sources for the Gupta age: the Prayaga Prashasti, written by the court poet Harisena, and the travelogue of Faxian, a Buddhist pilgrim from China. (a) State one thing each source tells us. (b) Compare whose point of view each writer represents. (c) For each source, state one way its writer's position could limit or colour what he wrote. (d) Which source would you trust more for daily life in the cities, and which for Samudragupta's wars? Justify, and say what the historian should still do.
questions.a: (a) The Prashasti tells of Samudragupta's wars, his ambition to unify the Earth and his support for art, learning and trade; Faxian tells of happy, numerous people, salaried guards, rich cities and charity houses. (b) Harisena speaks for the king's court; Faxian is an outside visitor writing for people of his homeland. (c) Harisena wrote to praise his king, so defeats or harshness would be left out; Faxian saw only some places at one time and a limited part of society, and his excerpt leaves out the chandalas' harsh treatment. (d) Faxian is the better guide to city life because he observed it directly as an outsider; the Prashasti is the main record of the wars but is one-sided praise. In both cases the historian must corroborate with other sources such as coins, inscriptions and texts.
s: (a) One thing from each source
(b) Harisena: the court's view; Faxian: an outside visitor's view
(c) Prashasti written to praise; Faxian's view partial in place, time and group
(d) choice with reasons: Faxian for city life, Prashasti for wars
(d) corroboration: the historian still checks against other sources

questions.q: What was the primary source of revenue of the Gupta rulers?
questions.a: Land tax

questions.q: Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, was married to a prince of the Vakataka kingdom. Which idea of Kautilya, recalled in the chapter, does this marriage best illustrate?
questions.a: Forming alliances (mitra), one of the components of the saptanga
o: Forming alliances (mitra), one of the components of the saptanga
Collecting land tax as the main source of revenue
Recording land grants on copper plates
Taking grand titles such as samrat and chakravartin

questions.q:
Read the statements about Gupta administration.
I. The Guptas divided their empire into provinces instead of controlling everything from a central authority.
II. Many copper plates recording Gupta land grants have been discovered by archaeologists in recent times.
III. Land was granted to local rulers, priests and chieftains.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III

questions.q: True or False: 'Prabhavati Gupta was the daughter of Samudragupta.' Correct the statement if needed.
questions.a: False. Prabhavati Gupta was the daughter of Chandragupta II; Samudragupta, Chandragupta II's father, was her grandfather.
s: States the verdict: False
Correction: she was the daughter of Chandragupta II (Samudragupta was her grandfather)

questions.q:
(a) Name any two goods that India exported in the Gupta era.
(b) Name any one region outside India with which it traded.
questions.a: (a) Any two of textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones. (b) Any one of the Mediterranean world, Southeast Asia and China.
s: (a) Any two of textiles, spices, ivory, gemstones
(b) Mediterranean world, Southeast Asia or China

questions.q:
Answer these questions on the titles of Gupta rulers.
(a) Name two titles adopted by Gupta rulers.
(b) Name one simpler title used by earlier rulers.
(c) From which two kinds of sources do we learn about these titles?
questions.a: (a) Any two of maharajadhiraja, samrat and chakravartin. (b) Rajan or maharaja. (c) Inscriptions and coins.
s: (a) Any two of maharajadhiraja, samrat, chakravartin
(b) Rajan or maharaja
(c) Inscriptions and coins

questions.q:
A newly appointed Gupta governor must run a large, distant province. Adviser 1 says: 'Send our own officials to every village and decide everything from the capital.' Adviser 2 says: 'Grant land to local rulers, priests and chieftains, and record every grant on copper plates.'
(a) Which adviser's plan matches the way the Gupta Empire was actually run?
(b) Give two benefits the chapter links to that system.
(c) Why were the grants inscribed on copper plates, and how do we know today that they were?
(d) Decide which plan the governor should follow, giving one reason for it and one risk it could carry.
questions.a: (a) Adviser 2: instead of controlling everything from a central authority, the Guptas divided the empire into provinces and granted land to local rulers, priests and chieftains. (b) It helped ensure proper tax collection, and it let the Gupta rulers govern efficiently while local leaders kept some control over their regions. (c) To keep accurate records; many such copper plates have been discovered by archaeologists in recent times. (d) Adviser 2's plan: the chapter says this system gave efficient rule and proper tax collection over a vast empire. A risk (reasoned inference): local leaders who keep power can grow strong, and by the 6th century CE the rise of powerful regional rulers led to internal conflicts. Accept a reasoned decision that weighs both.
s: (a) Adviser 2: provinces and land grants, not central control
(b) Proper tax collection; efficient rule with some local control
(c) Accurate records; many copper plates found by archaeologists
(d) Decision with one reason for and one risk (e.g. regional rulers grew strong)

questions.q:
A Nagpur school plans a heritage walk to Ramagiri (Ramtek hill), where some temples linked with a Gupta princess stand. The guide's notes say: 'She came from the Gupta court, married into the ruling family of this region and later ruled it for some years, though she was never its queen by birth. One of her inscriptions calls her a mother of two kings, and she is linked with seven temples.'
(a) Name the princess and her father.
(b) Which kingdom did she marry into, and where did it lie in relation to the Guptas?
(c) Explain how she could rule a kingdom 'though never its queen by birth'.
(d) The walk can add one sign: 'A marriage that conquered the Vakatakas' or 'A marriage that built an alliance'. Which is accurate? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II. (b) The Vakataka kingdom, the Guptas' neighbours to the south (in the central part of the subcontinent). (c) Her husband, the Vakataka prince, died early, so she ruled as regent until her sons could take the throne. (d) 'A marriage that built an alliance': the chapter treats such marriages as matrimonial alliances, the Vakatakas were allies of the Guptas, and she kept the ties between the two strong; nothing says the Vakatakas were conquered.
s: (a) Prabhavati Gupta, daughter of Chandragupta II
(b) The Vakataka kingdom, south of the Guptas
(c) Ruled as regent after her husband's early death
(d) Alliance, because the Vakatakas were allies and ties stayed strong

questions.q: Imagine you are a Gupta provincial officer writing a report to the maharajadhiraja. (a) Name the three methods the Gupta rulers used to expand and consolidate their empire. (b) List three sources of revenue you collect and two things the revenue is spent on. (c) Name two goods leaving through the ports and one stop on the sea route to the Mediterranean. (d) The treasury can fund only one new project: better roads to the ports, or new irrigation works for farmland. Recommend one, giving a reason from what the chapter says about revenue and a reason from what it says about trade.
questions.a: (a) Military conquests, diplomacy and alliances (including matrimonial alliances). (b) Any three of land tax, fines, taxes on mines, irrigation, trade and crafts; any two of administration, the army, building temples and infrastructure, supporting scholars and artists. (c) Any two of textiles, spices, ivory and gemstones; Socotra Island in the Arabian Sea. (d) Either choice, if both reasons are used: land tax was the primary source of revenue, and irrigation is itself taxed, so farmland matters most for revenue; but the chapter says such an empire had to promote vibrant internal and external trade to sustain itself, and trade and crafts were also taxed. A recommendation that weighs the two and justifies its choice earns full marks.
s: (a) Military conquests, diplomacy, alliances
(b) Three revenue sources and two uses
(c) Two exports and Socotra
(d) Revenue reason: land tax the primary source (irrigation taxed)
(d) Trade reason and a justified recommendation weighing both

questions.q: Which scholar of the Gupta period wrote the encyclopedic Brihat Samhita?
questions.a: Varahamihira

questions.q:
Match each name in Column A with the correct description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Aryabhata  2. Varahamihira  3. Kalidasa  4. Charaka Samhita
Column B: A. A text dealing with diagnosing diseases, treatments and diet  B. Poet of 'The Cloud Messenger'  C. Lived in Kusumapura, near present-day Patna  D. Lived in Ujjayini

Assertion (A): Aryabhata gave an explanation for the alternation of day and night.
Reason (R): Aryabhata proposed that the Sun moves around the Earth once every day.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) What does the word 'codified' mean?
(b) Name the two Ayurveda texts that were compiled and given their final shape in the Gupta period.
questions.a: (a) Arranged or written in an organised and systematic way. (b) The Charaka Samhita and the Sushruta Samhita.
s: (a) Arranged or written in an organised, systematic way
(b) Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita

questions.q:
(a) In which city did Varahamihira live?
(b) Name any two subjects covered in his Brihat Samhita.
questions.a: (a) Ujjayini. (b) Any two of astronomy, astrology, weather forecasting, architecture, town planning and farming.
s: (a) Ujjayini
(b) Any two subjects of the Brihat Samhita

questions.q:
Answer these about Kalidasa's Meghadutam.
(a) What does the title mean in English?
(b) Why does the yaksha send a message through a passing cloud?
(c) Apart from emotions of love, what does the poem describe in great detail?
questions.a: (a) 'The Cloud Messenger'. (b) He has been banished from his home by his master and sends a message to his beloved through the cloud. (c) The landscapes and weather of north India on the cloud's journey.
s: (a) The Cloud Messenger
(b) Banished from home, he sends a message to his beloved
(c) The landscapes and weather of north India

questions.q: Complete this chain from the chapter in three links, explaining each: Long peace and stability -> ? -> ? -> Achievements such as the works of Aryabhata and Kalidasa.
questions.a: Link 1: Peace and stability strengthened the economy. Link 2: A stronger economy allowed the state to support scholars, artists and scientists; Chandragupta II, for example, kept many learned men, poets and artists at his court. Link 3: This patronage led to cultural and intellectual growth, so new works in science and literature were produced.
s: Peace strengthened the economy
The state could support scholars, artists and scientists (patronage, e.g. Chandragupta II's court)
Patronage led to cultural and intellectual growth and new works

questions.q:
For a 'Roots of Science' exhibition in Ujjain, the district office will show five present-day departments: the weather office, the town-planning office, the agriculture office, the district hospital and an observatory. Each panel will show one Gupta-age work linked to those departments.
(a) Which single Gupta-age work links to the largest number of these departments? Name the departments it covers.
(b) Which department needs a different work, and which work?
(c) Which scholar of the observatory panel lived in this very city?
(d) The office can afford only two panels but wants all five departments covered. Is that possible? Justify, and say which scholar's work would then be left out.
questions.a: (a) Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita: it covers astronomy, weather forecasting, town planning and farming, so it links to the observatory, weather, town-planning and agriculture offices (4 of 5). (b) The district hospital needs an Ayurveda text such as the Charaka Samhita or Sushruta Samhita. (c) Varahamihira, who lived in Ujjayini. (d) Yes: the Brihat Samhita (4 departments) plus an Ayurveda Samhita (the hospital) cover all 5 with two panels; Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya would be left out even though it is a major astronomy work.
s: (a) Brihat Samhita, covering weather, town planning, farming and astronomy
(b) Hospital: Charaka or Sushruta Samhita
(c) Varahamihira of Ujjayini
(d) Yes, two panels cover all five; the Aryabhatiya is left out

questions.q: A class debate takes the motion: 'Peace did more than any single king to create the classical age of the Guptas.' Using the chapter: (a) explain how peace led to patronage; (b) give one example from science; (c) one from literature; (d) one from medicine; (e) judge the motion, taking into account the role of Chandragupta II.
questions.a: (a) The long peace and stability strengthened the economy, letting the state support scholars, artists and scientists. (b) Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya, or Varahamihira's Brihat Samhita. (c) Kalidasa's Sanskrit poetry such as the Meghadutam, or the compiling of major Puranas. (d) The Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas given their final shape. (e) A balanced judgement: the chapter credits the 'prolonged period of peace and stability' for the achievements, but it also says the fields flourished particularly in the time of Chandragupta II, who surrounded himself with learned men, poets and artists; peace made patronage possible and rulers chose to use it, so the motion is largely but not wholly right.
s: (a) Peace -> stronger economy -> support for scholars and artists
(b) A science example
(c) A literature example
(d) A medicine example
(e) Judgement weighing peace against Chandragupta II's patronage

questions.q: Which centre of Gupta art, near Varanasi in present-day Uttar Pradesh, is known for its exquisite sculptures of the Buddha?
questions.a: Sarnath

questions.q: A museum shows a Gupta-period terracotta figure from Ahichchhatra of a river goddess with water flowing over her head and a pot beside her. She stands on a tortoise. Which identification is correct, and what settles it?
questions.a: Yamuna, because the tortoise is her vahana
o: Yamuna, because the tortoise is her vahana
Ganga, because water flows over her head
Ganga, because the tortoise is her vahana
Yamuna, because she is shown with a pot

questions.q:
Read the statements about the decline of the Guptas.
I. The chapter presents attacks from outside as the only challenge the later Gupta rulers faced.
II. The rise of powerful regional rulers led to internal conflicts.
III. By the 6th century CE the Gupta Empire began showing signs of decline.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: A museum label under a Gupta-period terracotta river goddess from Ahichchhatra, who stands on a tortoise, reads: 'Ganga, recognised by the water flowing over her head.' True or False? Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: False. Water flows over the heads of both river goddesses, so it cannot tell them apart; their vahanas do. The figure on a tortoise is Yamuna, while Ganga stands on a makara (a mythical creature akin to a crocodile).
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: water is shown on both; the tortoise marks Yamuna, Ganga stands on a makara

questions.q: For each of these centres of Gupta art, write the present-day state it is in and one thing it is known for: (a) Sarnath, (b) Ajanta, (c) Udayagiri.
questions.a: (a) Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh: sculptures of the Buddha. (b) Ajanta, Maharashtra: caves with paintings and sculpture, carved with the support of the Guptas and Vakatakas. (c) Udayagiri, Madhya Pradesh: rock-cut caves and detailed carvings of deities.
s: (a) Uttar Pradesh; Buddha sculptures
(b) Maharashtra; cave art (paintings, cave-temples)
(c) Madhya Pradesh; rock-cut caves and carvings of deities

questions.q: A student must support the claim that 'Gupta art set high standards of beauty' with examples from the chapter. (a)-(c) Name the place and say what the work shows for one example each of: (a) sculpture of the Buddha, (b) painting, (c) terracotta. (d) Which of your three examples best shows the skill of the artists, and why?
questions.a: (a) Sarnath, near Varanasi: exquisite sculptures of the Buddha. (b) Ajanta, Maharashtra: a painting of Bodhisattva Padmapani. (c) Ahichchhatra, western Uttar Pradesh: terracotta figures of the river goddesses Ganga on a makara and Yamuna on a tortoise. (d) Any one with a sensible reason tied to the chapter, e.g. the Sarnath sculptures, which the chapter itself calls exquisite; or the Ahichchhatra terracottas, where small details (vahanas, water over the heads, the pot) let a viewer tell the two rivers apart.
s: (a) Sarnath: Buddha sculptures
(b) Ajanta: painting of Bodhisattva Padmapani
(c) Ahichchhatra: terracotta Ganga and Yamuna
(d) A choice with a reason drawn from the chapter

questions.q:
A school role-play is set in a Gupta court in the 6th century CE. The king's advisers bring two reports. Report 1: 'A fierce tribe keeps raiding our lands in the north; each raid weakens our hold there.' Report 2: 'Two strong local rulers who once paid us tribute now act on their own and fight each other.'
(a) Name the tribe in Report 1 and the region it came from.
(b) Which cause of decline from the chapter does Report 2 show?
(c) Using what the chapter says about how Samudragupta treated many defeated kings, explain why such local rulers could become strong.
(d) One adviser says, 'Defeat the raiders and the empire is safe.' Evaluate this advice.
questions.a: (a) The Hunas, from Central Asia. (b) The rise of powerful regional rulers, leading to internal conflicts. (c) Many defeated kings were reinstated and only paid tribute, so they kept their own kingdoms and power; such rulers could later grow strong and act on their own. (d) The advice is incomplete: the chapter names two causes working at the same time, external Huna attacks and internal conflicts from rising regional rulers, so defeating the Hunas alone would not remove the danger from within.
s: (a) The Hunas, from Central Asia
(b) Rise of powerful regional rulers causing internal conflicts
(c) Reinstated tributary kings kept their own power and could grow strong
(d) Advice incomplete: internal conflicts remain a second cause

questions.q:
Answer these questions on Gupta art and the decline of the empire.
(a) At which site in present-day Uttar Pradesh does the chapter show a sculpture of Vishnu on Sheshnag?
(b) What rises from the central stupa in the Ajanta cave that replicates a temple?
(c) What is shown in the famous Ajanta painting mentioned in the chapter?
(d) By which century did the Gupta Empire begin to show signs of decline?
(e) Name the tribe whose repeated attacks weakened the empire's control over north India.
questions.a: (a) Deogarh (the Dashavatara temple). (b) A seated Buddha. (c) Bodhisattva Padmapani. (d) The 6th century CE. (e) The Hunas (from central Asia).
s: (a) Deogarh
(b) A seated Buddha
(c) Bodhisattva Padmapani
(d) 6th century CE
(e) The Hunas

questions.q: Aman writes: 'The Pallava dynasty was created by Samudragupta after his southern campaign.' Which fact from the chapter shows this is wrong?
questions.a: The Pallavas appear to have been a tributary power under the Satavahanas and gained power as the Satavahanas declined.
o: The Pallavas appear to have been a tributary power under the Satavahanas and gained power as the Satavahanas declined.
Most of the Pallavas were devotees of Shiva, while the Guptas followed Vishnu.
Kanchipuram is often known as the 'city of a thousand temples'.
The Kamarupa kingdom was ruled by the Varman dynasty.

questions.q:
Match each power in Column A with the fact about it in Column B, as given in the chapter.
Column A: 1. Pallavas  2. Kamarupa kingdom  3. Vakatakas  4. Gupta Empire
Column B: A. Ruled in parts of present-day Assam  B. Capital at Pataliputra (present-day Patna)  C. Rose to power after the Satavahana dynasty  D. Capital at Nandivardhana, near present-day Nagpur

Assertion (A): Kanchipuram developed as one of the major centres of learning in the south.
Reason (R): Most of the Pallava rulers were devotees of Shiva.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
(a) Which dynasty ruled the Kamarupa kingdom?
(b) Over which river valley did the Kamarupa kingdom extend?
questions.a: (a) The Varman dynasty. (b) The Brahmaputra valley (broadly, present-day Assam).
s: (a) The Varman dynasty
(b) The Brahmaputra valley

questions.q:
Answer briefly about the Pallavas.
(a) What was their capital?
(b) Which god were most of them devoted to?
(c) Name any two present-day states where they consolidated their power.
questions.a: (a) Kanchipuram (in present-day Tamil Nadu). (b) Shiva. (c) Any two of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.
s: (a) Kanchipuram
(b) Shiva
(c) Any two of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh

questions.q: The chapter discusses ghatikas while describing Pallava Kanchipuram, but it says ghatikas emerged during the reign of the Satavahanas. Explain (a) what ghatikas were, (b) how they link the two dynasties, and (c) what this suggests about how the Pallavas built their power and culture.
questions.a: (a) Ghatikas were centres of learning. (b) They emerged under the Satavahanas, and the Pallavas, who appear to have been a tributary power under the Satavahanas, continued to benefit from them as Kanchipuram grew into a major centre of learning. (c) The Pallavas built on what came before: they rose as the Satavahanas declined and carried forward older institutions, adding their own temples and rock-cut caves.
s: (a) Ghatikas were centres of learning
(b) Began under the Satavahanas and fostered learning in Pallava Kanchipuram
(c) The Pallavas built on earlier institutions as they rose after the Satavahanas

questions.q:
Pen-friends in Guwahati and Kanchipuram write about their regions' past. The Guwahati letter says: 'Our valley appears in the Ramayana and Mahabharata under an ancient name, and in Gupta times our kings' temples and monasteries were hubs of learning.' The Kanchipuram letter says: 'Our city was the capital of a southern dynasty that ruled till the latter half of the 9th century CE.'
(a) Name the kingdom and the ruling dynasty of the Guwahati region in this period.
(b) Give the ancient name of the valley.
(c) What did Samudragupta do to the rulers of both regions?
(d) The Guwahati student adds, 'So our region was simply part of the Gupta Empire.' Is this right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The Kamarupa kingdom, ruled by the Varman dynasty. (b) Pragjyotisha. (c) He defeated a Pallava ruler and the ruler of Kamarupa but did not take direct control; he let them keep their thrones as long as they accepted his rule and paid tribute. (d) Only partly right: Kamarupa accepted Gupta supremacy and paid tribute, but it kept its own rulers and was not directly governed as part of the empire.
s: (a) Kamarupa, Varman dynasty
(b) Pragjyotisha
(c) Defeated them but let them keep their thrones on accepting his rule and paying tribute
(d) Partly right: tributary under Gupta supremacy, not directly ruled

questions.q: 'Samudragupta was wise not to take direct control of the Pallava and Kamarupa kingdoms.' Evaluate this statement. (a) State what he did after defeating their rulers. (b) Give the effect on relations that the chapter names. (c) The Gupta Empire flourished till the 6th century CE and the Pallavas ruled till the latter half of the 9th century CE: roughly how much longer did Pallava rule last? (d) Give one argument against the statement, using the chapter's account of the Gupta decline. (e) Give your verdict.
questions.a: (a) He let the rulers keep their thrones as long as they accepted his rule and paid tribute. (b) The chapter says this helped maintain peaceful relations. (c) From about 600 CE to some time in 851-900 CE: roughly two and a half to three centuries longer. (d) Kings left with their own power could grow strong; by the 6th century CE the rise of powerful regional rulers caused internal conflicts that weakened the empire. (e) A reasoned verdict, for example: wise in the short run, since it brought tribute and peace without the cost of ruling distant lands, but it left strong regional powers that outlasted the Guptas.
s: (a) Kept their thrones on accepting his rule and paying tribute
(b) It helped maintain peaceful relations
(c) About two and a half to three centuries longer
(d) Argument against: strong regional rulers later caused internal conflicts
(e) A reasoned verdict weighing both sides
